newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says Israel needs to "get real" for peace.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says Israel needs to "get real" for peace.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said on Saturday that Israel needed to "get real" if it wanted peace in the region and warned that the only way to end violence was to address the reasons behind it.

Speaking to Israel's Channel Two in an interview broadcast in Egypt and Israel, Mubarak said that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, by not implementing peace deals signed with the Palestinians, had made the region unstable.

"I can assure you that Arafat doesn't dare to give these terrorist groups an order to blow something up. No one has the power to control terrorism," Mubarak said, referring to the Tel Aviv suicide bombing last week that killed three Israelis and was claimed by the Islamist Palestinian militant group Hamas.
Israel has accused Palestinian President Yasser Arafat of giving a tacit "green light" for militant attacks. The PLO denies the charge.
"You (Israel) have to look for the reasons rather than who did it. You have to find solutions so that the people can live in safety and peace," he added.
"Let's play another game, let's get real if we want peace," Mubarak said.

Israeli-PLO talks have been in crisis since Netanyahu broke ground last week on a Jewish settlement in disputed Arab East Jerusalem. This has sparked 10 days of non-stop violence in Palestinian self-rule West Bank.
On Saturday, a Palestinian became the first fatality of the clashes after he was shot in the back by Israeli troops in the West Bank.

Egypt, which considers itself the unofficial sponsor of the peace talks, held crisis talks last week on the settlement and Arab leaders have since condemned the project in an Islamic conference in Islamabad and a meeting of the Jerusalem Committee in Rabat.

Many countries say the 6,500 house settlement contradicts the 1993 Oslo peace agreement, which says that no one should take any action to change the demographic or geographic composition of Jersualem before its final status is negotiated.

But Netanyahu, who was elected on a platform that refuses to handover occupied Arab lands for peace as stipulated by a 1991 Madrid peace treaty, has said the project was just a way to solve the housing problem in Jerusalem.

Mubarak told the interviewers that Israel was responsible for the violence and unrest because of its lack of committment and that it could easily solve the thorny issue of Jeruslem if it implemented other peace pledges.
"If the treaties were implemented, then the Israeli people would not feel...concerned and worried, the Arabs are also feeling concerned and worried," he said.
"This violence is more dangerous than war and will affect not only Israel, but all of us involved in the peace process," he added.
Egypt in 1979 became the first Arab country to make peace with Israel but official relations remain cool.

Mubarak, who took over after president Anwar Sadat was assassinated in 1981, has yet to visit the Jewish state and he told the interviewer he would only do so after "the agreements are respected and justice is done".
